section.title: A Picture That Takes Work
section.para: Some pictures take a lot of computing. This one asks every point of the picture how soon it runs away when a little sum is repeated on it — the Mandelbrot set. The work is one for over the points, and the rounds of that loop do not depend on each other.

So nothing in the program says how it runs, and below the program you can choose: on one core of your computer, on all of them, or on the graphics card. The picture is the same; the time is not. relaxed lets the card compute a little less strictly.
section.programlisting:
function colour(x: i32, y: i32, w: i32, h: i32) returns u32 { let cr (x as f32) * 3.0 / (w as f32) - 2.1 let ci (y as f32) * 2.0 / (h as f32) - 1.0 var zr: f32 0.0 var zi: f32 0.0 var k: i32 0 while k < 200 and zr * zr + zi * zi <= 4.0 { let t zr * zr - zi * zi + cr zi := zr * 2.0 * zi + ci zr := t k := k + 1 } if k = 200 return 0xFF000000 let shade ((k % 32) * 8) as u32 0xFF000000 | ((255 - shade) << 16) | ((shade / 2) << 8) | shade }
let w: i32 600 let h: i32 400 var picture Vector[u32]((w * h) as size_t) relaxed for p in w * h picture.put(p as size_t, colour(p % w, p / w, w, h)) File.write_bytes("mandelbrot.`w`x`h`.rgba", picture.as_bytes()) print "`w * h` points"
section.para: The colour of a point is a number with four bytes — red, green, blue and how opaque it is — and the picture goes into a file whose name says its size; the playground shows such a file. The Mandelbrot showcase lets you zoom into it and race the cores against the card.
